title: What California's Right to Repair Act Means for New Construction Buyers
content_html:
What Is the Right to Repair Act?

California's Right to Repair Act, originally enacted as Senate Bill 800 and codified in the California Civil Code, establishes construction standards for new residential units and a specific process homeowners must generally follow before suing a builder over certain construction defects. [1] If you're buying new construction in Temecula Valley, Murrieta, or Menifee, understanding this law helps you know what protections come with your new home and what steps are involved if something goes wrong after you move in.

The law applies to residential construction where the purchase agreement was signed after January 1, 2003, and it covers single-family homes as well as condominiums. [2] It does not apply to every type of construction defect claim — it is specifically structured around a list of functional standards the home must meet.

The Functionality Standards

Rather than leaving "defect" to be argued case by case in every dispute, the statute lays out detailed, itemized standards covering specific building components and systems — things like water intrusion through windows and doors, foundation and structural performance, plumbing and sewer lines, electrical systems, and soil movement, among many other categories. [3] If a condition in the home does not meet the listed standard for that component, it can form the basis of a claim under the Act, generally without the homeowner having to separately prove that the condition caused property damage.

These standards are detailed and technical, and they vary significantly by building component. A buyer evaluating a potential issue in their new home should review the specific standard that applies to that component rather than assuming a general definition of "defect" governs the situation.

The Pre-Litigation Process

One of the most significant features of the Right to Repair Act is that it generally requires homeowners to follow a specific pre-litigation process before filing a lawsuit against the builder for a violation of the construction standards. [4] In broad terms, this process involves the homeowner giving the builder written notice of the claimed violation, after which the builder has an opportunity to inspect the property and, in many cases, to offer a repair.

The statute sets out the builder's obligations and the homeowner's obligations at each stage of this process, including timeframes for the builder to respond, inspect, and make a repair offer. Because the exact timeframes, notice requirements, and procedural steps are specific and detailed in the statute itself, a homeowner who believes they have a claim should review the actual code sections governing the process — or speak with an attorney — rather than relying on a general summary, since missing a procedural step can affect a homeowner's rights.

What This Means in Practice for Buyers

For a buyer purchasing new construction, the Right to Repair Act's practical significance is that it creates a structured path for addressing certain defects that doesn't necessarily require immediate litigation. The pre-litigation process is designed to give the builder a chance to fix a documented problem, which can sometimes result in a faster resolution than a lawsuit would.

That said, the Act is a complex statute with specific standards, notice requirements, and exceptions, and how it applies can depend heavily on the facts of a particular situation — including what was in the purchase agreement, whether any standards were enhanced or modified by agreement, and the nature of the condition itself. Buyers who encounter a potential construction defect in a newly built home should keep thorough records (photos, dates, communications with the builder) and consult with a qualified real estate or construction attorney to understand how the law applies to their specific circumstances.

Builder Warranties and the Right to Repair Act

Many production builders also provide their own limited warranties covering workmanship, systems, and structural components for specified periods after closing. These warranties are separate from, and often work alongside, the protections in the Right to Repair Act. When buying new construction, it's worth reading the builder's warranty documents carefully at the time of purchase so you understand what's covered, for how long, and what steps the warranty itself requires if an issue comes up — these documents often have their own notice and claim procedures distinct from the statutory pre-litigation process.

If you're comparing a newly built home to an existing resale property, it's also worth thinking through how warranty coverage, construction standards, and the overall buying process differ between the two — a topic covered in more detail in our comparison of new construction and resale homes in Temecula Valley.

Documentation Matters From Day One

Because so much of the Right to Repair process depends on written notice, inspection timing, and documented communication, buyers of new construction benefit from starting good documentation habits as soon as they take possession. Keep copies of the purchase agreement, any builder warranty documents, the final walkthrough checklist, and any correspondence about issues discovered after closing. If a problem does surface, having a clear, dated record of when it was noticed and how it was reported can matter a great deal if the pre-litigation process is ever invoked.

A home inspection — even on new construction — can also help identify issues early, before they become larger problems. The general principles covered in our guide to home inspections for first-time buyers apply to newly built homes as well, even though builders are required to meet their own set of construction standards.

Working With an Agent When Buying New Construction

Buying directly from a builder is a different process than buying a resale home, and the purchase contracts builders use are typically drafted by the builder's own legal team, often with different contingencies and timelines than a standard resale purchase agreement. Having an agent review the contract terms with you, and understanding what warranty and statutory protections apply before you sign, can help you go into the transaction with clear expectations.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does the Right to Repair Act cover every type of construction problem?

No. The Act is built around a specific, itemized list of construction standards covering particular building components and systems. Whether a given condition qualifies depends on which standard applies and whether the condition fails to meet it, which is why reviewing the actual statutory language — or consulting an attorney — matters for any specific situation.

Do I have to go through the pre-litigation process before suing a builder?

In general, the Act requires homeowners to follow its pre-litigation procedures before filing suit for a violation of the construction standards it covers. The exact requirements and exceptions are detailed in the statute itself, and an attorney can advise on how they apply to a specific claim.

Does a builder's own warranty replace the Right to Repair Act?

No — a builder's limited warranty and the statutory protections under the Right to Repair Act are generally separate. It's worth understanding both: what the builder's warranty document says it covers, and what the statute requires independent of that warranty.
